whatItDoes: Estimates the future value of a Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) — equal monthly amounts invested at a projected annual return. Breaks the result into the amount invested versus the estimated returns earned, and lets you adjust the contribution, rate, and duration to compare scenarios.
whyItExists: SIPs are the standard way most people invest in mutual funds. The growth curve from fixed monthly contributions is unintuitive, so a calculator turns the recurring-investment formula into an easy-to-read maturity value and shows how much of it is your own money.
whoShouldUse: Mutual fund investors, first-time investors planning monthly deposits, salary earners automating savings, and anyone comparing SIP amounts or durations for a financial goal.
useCases: Estimate the maturity value of a monthly SIP before committing to a fund
Compare different monthly contributions and durations side by side
Understand how much of the final value is returns vs. invested capital
Model retirement accumulation from monthly investing
Set a target and reverse-engineer the monthly amount needed to reach it
Decide how long to keep a SIP running before a large expense
instructions: Set the expected annual return rate in percent
Choose how many years you will keep investing
Read the matured value, total invested, and estimated returns
Adjust the monthly amount to find a contribution that reaches your goal
Optionally switch contribution timing to match when your SIP is debited
examples: $5,000/month at 12% for 10 years → ~$1.14M matured, of which ~$600,000 is invested
$2,000/month at 10% for 15 years → ~$829,000 matured, of which ~$360,000 is invested
$1,000/month at 8% for 20 years → ~$589,000 matured, of which ~$240,000 is invested
$5,000/month at 12% for 20 years → ~$4.95M matured vs. ~$1.2M invested — returns dwarf contributions
bestPractices: Treat the return rate as an expected long-run average, not a guarantee
Keep investing through market downs and ups to capture the full cycle
Review your SIP amount as your income grows and step it up
Use the total-invested figure to check how much of the final value comes from your own money
Start early — the same monthly amount compounds to far more over 20 years than 10
commonMistakes: Using short-term past returns as the long-term expectation
Stopping the SIP during market dips, which locks in losses and skips cheap units
Forgetting inflation shrinks the purchase power of the final amount
Entering a monthly amount when you actually contribute quarterly
Ignoring expense ratios and exit loads, which reduce net returns
faq: Is the SIP projection guaranteed? — No, returns are assumed and can be lower or higher.
Can I use this for non-mutual-fund investing? — Yes, the math is the same for any monthly-return plan.
Does it account for fund charges? — No, expense ratios and taxes are not included.
Is my data sent anywhere? — No, everything runs locally in your browser.
What is contribution timing? — It controls whether each contribution is invested at the start or end of the month; start-of-month matches how most SIPs are debited.
Should I stop my SIP when markets fall? — Historically, staying invested through downturns has been key to capturing long-term equity returns.
assumptions: Generic SIP/recurring investment calculation; no country-specific assumptions.
faq: Does this tool support multiple currencies? — Yes, select your currency from the dropdown. All calculations run locally in your browser.
